candidates.attacker_control: The public JobStatusStore API accepts List<String> identifiers for getJobStatus, remove, and createLoggerTail, and AbstractRequest#setId(List<String>) / setId(String...) publicly preserve arbitrary caller-supplied segments. Job request IDs are then used by AbstractJob.initialize() to create the job log and by DefaultJobStatusStore.store() to persist status. In a downstream application that maps a request path, script parameter, or generic job request to these APIs, an attacker controls the list elements and can supply '..'. No validation or trust-boundary check is present in this module.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: URLEncoder does encode '/', '\\', '%', and NUL, so a single ID element cannot carry an embedded multi-segment path; a lone '.'/'..' element is required, and multiple list elements are needed to climb multiple levels. The in-repo FilterStreamConverterJobRequest and ExtensionRequest builders use fixed prefixes and at most two variable path segments, which limits how far those specific requests can traverse; this finding therefore depends on a generic or direct caller accepting an arbitrary ID list. The status file name is fixed to status.xml/status.zip, and the attacker needs filesystem write access for the status-deserialization variant. No downstream HTTP endpoint, runtime behavior, or XStream gadget availability was confirmed in this snapshot.
candidates.impact: If the API is exposed with attacker-controlled IDs, this permits deletion or truncation of directories and files outside the job-status storage, including the permanent XWiki data directory or other application files. It also permits status/log reads from unintended locations and can turn an existing attacker-writable status.xml/status.zip into unsafe XStream deserialization, with possible code execution depending on the classpath. Even without the RCE condition, the directory-deletion primitive is a high-impact availability/integrity issue.
candidates.prerequisites: A caller reachable by the attacker must pass an untrusted job-ID list to JobStatusStore/JobManager or execute a generic Request with such an ID. For directory deletion, the traversed target must exist and the XWiki process must have permission to delete it. For the deserialization impact, an attacker-controlled status.xml or status.zip must already be present at a path reachable through the traversal, and a gadget must be available on the classpath; neither condition is proven by this snapshot alone. Fixed in-repo job constructors often limit the number of variable segments, so the strongest impact requires a generic or direct ID-list caller.
candidates.root_cause: DefaultJobStatusStore.encode() relies on URLEncoder alone. URLEncoder percent-encodes separators such as '/' and '\\' but leaves '.' and '..' unchanged. getJobFolder() then appends each encoded job-ID element with new File(folder, element) and never normalizes the result or checks that it remains under the configured storage directory. Consequently, a job-ID element of '..' resolves to the parent directory. The public remove(List<String>) method recursively deletes the resolved directory with FileUtils.deleteDirectory(); getJobStatus(List<String>) reads status.zip/status.xml from the resolved directory; and createLoggerTail(List<String>) initializes log files there. JobStatusSerializer.read() then unmarshals the traversed status file with SafeXStream, which deliberately does not enable XStream's class whitelist. The root cause is the missing path-element validation/containment check, not merely the XStream behavior that amplifies it.
candidates.title: Path traversal in job status storage via unneutralized dot-segments in job IDs
candidates.trace: 1) Caller supplies an ID list containing a '..' segment. 2) DefaultJobStatusStore.encode() calls URLEncoder.encode(); '..' stays '..'. 3) getJobFolder() performs new File(folder, encodedElement) for every segment without normalize()/toRealPath()/startsWith containment. 4) remove() calls FileUtils.deleteDirectory(jobFolder) on that resolved path. 5) getJobStatus() reads status.zip/status.xml from the resolved path and JobStatusSerializer.read() passes it to SafeXStream.fromXML(); SafeXStream.initialize() explicitly does not call setupDefaultSecurity(), so reflection-based unmarshalling has no class whitelist. 6) createLoggerTail() similarly opens/truncates log.log and log.index at the resolved path when a serializable job is initialized.
candidates.unverified: The assigned source does not contain the downstream XWiki Platform REST/script endpoint or other caller that passes external job IDs to JobStatusStore, so remote reachability and required privileges are unverified. No runtime test or exploit was executed. Whether the available classpath contains an XStream gadget and whether an attacker can place a suitable status XML at a traversed path are also unverified.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

coverage_summary: get_source_scope reported 1,409 model-visible source files, with no files excluded for size, sensitive names/paths, or symlinks; no binary files were skipped during the searches. I inventoried the core modules and reviewed high-risk code and sinks in job, filter, XML/XStream, diff, netflux/websocket, extension, classloader, script, velocity, crypto, environment, cache, and repository modules. I also searched for process execution, reflection/class loading, XML parser configuration, path handling, URL/network access, file output, XStream, cryptographic randomness, and script-service exposure. This was not a line-by-line review of all 1,409 files, and the snapshot contains no test sources or downstream platform modules.
limitations: No runtime execution, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were used; all conclusions are source-level leads.

The snapshot is XWiki Commons only. Downstream XWiki Platform endpoints that may expose job IDs, filter properties, or HTML diffing were not available, so true remote reachability and authorization requirements are unverified.

Some candidate impact depends on dependency/library behavior (DOM parser feature support, XStream gadget availability, Apache Commons IO deletion semantics) that was inferred from source rather than executed.
The source snapshot has no test files, making intended security semantics and existing regression coverage uninspectable.
Dependency contents and runtime classpath were not inspected beyond the POM declarations.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtils.parse() apparently permits DOCTYPE declarations by setting the Xerces disallow-doctype-decl feature to false despite the anti-XXE comment.
rejected_leads.reason: Suspicious and worth a separate review, but external DTD loading and external general/parameter entity features are also set to false; whether the configured DOM parser honors those parameters and whether an in-scope caller feeds raw attacker XML are unverified. Residual entity-expansion DoS remains possible but was not demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultExtensionSerializer uses a default DocumentBuilderFactory without XXE hardening while parsing extension descriptors.
rejected_leads.reason: The parser is clearly unhardened, but in this snapshot the descriptor sources are local, generated, or reached through extension-management operations that already carry a high trust/admin requirement; no low-privilege in-scope parse path was established.

rejected_leads.lead: SafeXStream intentionally does not enable an XStream class whitelist and SafeMessageConverter accepts XML class attributes.
rejected_leads.reason: This is a dangerous deserializer, but all in-scope readers consume locally generated status/log/extension-history files. It was included as the impact amplifier in the selected path-traversal chain rather than submitted as an independent candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: HTMLImageEmbedder converts every img src to a data URI via DataURIConverter, which the interface says accesses the URL; DiffHTMLScriptService exposes unified HTML diffing with this filter in the default configuration.
rejected_leads.reason: The converter implementation is absent from this snapshot, so the protocol handling, network access, size limits, and any SSRF/local-file-read restrictions cannot be verified. The image URLs are attacker-influenced, but the fetching sink is outside the reviewed source.

rejected_leads.lead: Netflux Utils.getRandomHexString uses java.util.Random for channel keys, user IDs, and the history-keeper key.
rejected_leads.reason: This is a real cryptographic-quality concern because channel keys act as capabilities and Netflux has no separate authorization. However, each call creates an independent Random and no seed/key prediction from observed outputs was demonstrated, so the security impact is less concrete than the selected traversal.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultInputSourceReferenceParser and DefaultOutputTargetReferenceParser accept file:/url: references, potentially enabling local file read, SSRF, or file writes through filter conversion jobs.
rejected_leads.reason: The parsing is intentional for trusted filter configuration. The snapshot contains no low-privilege web/script caller that maps untrusted references into these properties, so this was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: LinkFilter does not treat protocol-relative URLs such as //example.com as external, so target=_blank links may avoid noopener/no-referrer.
rejected_leads.reason: The impact is reverse-tabnabbing/phishing rather than direct compromise, and the URI classification may be intentional; it is weaker than the selected issue.

rejected_leads.lead: LocalExtensionStorage builds filesystem paths from extension IDs and versions.
rejected_leads.reason: PathUtils.encode replaces '.' and '*' in addition to URL-encoding separators, so the obvious traversal segments are neutralized there.

summary: The strongest source-supported candidate is a path-traversal weakness in the job status store. Job ID segments are URL-encoded but dot segments are not neutralized, then joined to filesystem paths without containment. The same root cause reaches directory deletion, status/log writes, and status-file reads; the status serializer then uses a SafeXStream instance that intentionally has no class whitelist. Other parser, SSRF, PRNG, and file-reference leads were considered but not selected because their in-scope attacker path or downstream implementation is missing.
